Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.name: Bacterial spot
Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.summary: A bacterial leaf and fruit disease (Xanthomonas) that spreads in warm, wet weather through splashing water, contaminated seed and handling of wet plants.
symptoms: Small yellow-green, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown with yellow halos
Leaf drop in bad cases; raised, scabby spots on fruit
Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.cure_note: There is no cure once it is established. Management is about slowing spread and protecting new growth, so act early.
treatment: Remove and destroy heavily infected plants or leaves; do not handle the plants when they are wet
Apply a copper-based bactericide registered for peppers as a preventive spray, following the label. Copper alone used continuously gives only partial control
Water at the base (drip or soaker); avoid overhead irrigation
Keep fertility balanced; under-fed plants are hit harder
prevention: Plant resistant pepper varieties where available; this is the first line of defence
Start with disease-free seed and transplants and inspect seedlings often
Rotate away from peppers and tomatoes, remove crop debris and control weeds

sources.title: WVU Extension: Bacterial leaf spot of pepper
UF/IFAS EDIS PP362: Bacterial spot of pepper
Growing Produce (UGA Extension): Pepper growers must be proactive with bacterial spot

Pepper__bell___healthy.name: Healthy leaf
Pepper__bell___healthy.summary: No sign of the diseases this model knows about.
treatment: No treatment needed. Keep scouting leaves (including undersides) every few days
prevention: Water at the base in the morning so leaves dry quickly
Space plants for airflow, keep weeds down and remove fallen debris
Use resistant varieties and disease-free transplants next season

Potato___Early_blight.name: Early blight
Potato___Early_blight.summary: A fungal disease (Alternaria solani) that starts on older leaves, favoured by warm, humid weather and leaf wetness, and can also affect tubers.
symptoms: Brown leaf spots with concentric rings (a target look)
Older leaves yellow and die first; sunken dark lesions on tubers
Potato___Early_blight.cure_note: Spots already on a leaf do not heal, but the spread can be controlled and later growth protected.
treatment: Apply a protectant fungicide such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb on a 7-10 day schedule, depending on weather and the product label
After flowering, extension services recommend adding systemic fungicides for several sprays, rotating products by FRAC group to avoid resistance
Remove badly infected foliage and keep the crop well fed and watered; stressed plants are more susceptible
prevention: Rotate to non-host crops for at least 3 years (avoid tomato, eggplant and pepper in between)
Plant certified, disease-free seed; later-maturing varieties are less susceptible
Handle tubers gently and store lesion-free tubers cool, dry and ventilated

sources.title: NDSU Extension PP1892: Early blight of potato
University of Delaware Weekly Crop Update: early blight

Potato___Late_blight.name: Late blight
Potato___Late_blight.summary: A fast, destructive disease caused by Phytophthora infestans. Cool, wet weather favours it and a field can be defoliated within days to a few weeks.
symptoms: Water-soaked green to dark spots on leaves, often with pale halos, and dark lesions on stems
White fuzzy growth under leaves in humid weather; reddish-brown dry rot under the skin of tubers
Potato___Late_blight.cure_note: There is no cure. Control depends on prevention and on destroying infected tissue so it stops releasing spores.
treatment: Act at once: destroy infected plants or foliage so the pathogen cannot keep producing spores, and tell your local extension or agriculture office because it spreads between farms
Protectant fungicides must go on before infection and be repeated through wet spells; use products labelled for late blight and rotate FRAC groups
Kill vines completely before harvest and wait before digging tubers, and avoid bruising them
Store tubers cool and ventilated, and grade out suspect tubers
prevention: Plant only certified blight-free seed tubers
Destroy cull piles and volunteer potatoes, and control nightshade weeds
Avoid long leaf-wetness periods and watch local blight alerts

sources.title: NDSU Extension PP1849: Late blight in potato
UAF Extension: Control strategies for late blight
UMaine Extension Bulletin 2417: Protecting potato tubers from late blight

Potato___healthy.name: Healthy leaf
Potato___healthy.summary: No sign of the diseases this model knows about.
treatment: No treatment needed. Keep checking leaves weekly, especially after cool, wet weather
prevention: Use certified seed tubers and rotate crops
Remove volunteer potatoes and nightshade weeds
Avoid prolonged leaf wetness; irrigate in the morning

Tomato_Bacterial_spot.name: Bacterial spot
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.summary: A bacterial disease (Xanthomonas species) of leaves, stems and fruit that spreads by splashing water and on seed, transplants and hands.
symptoms: Small, angular dark spots on leaves, often with yellow halos
Raised, scabby spots on fruit
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.cure_note: There is no curative treatment. Preventive measures reduce spread but will not clear an infected plant.
treatment: Remove and destroy the worst infected plants and leaves; avoid working among wet plants
Preventive copper-based sprays are used in warm, wet periods, but copper-resistant strains are common, so copper is only a partial tool. Follow the product label and local advice
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering
prevention: Buy tested, disease-free seed and transplants; hot-water seed treatment can help
Wait at least a year before replanting tomatoes in the same spot and remove volunteer tomato plants
Clear and dispose of crop debris after harvest
No commercial tomato varieties are fully resistant, so keep other measures in place

sources.title: UW-Madison Extension Horticulture: Bacterial spot of tomato
Purdue Vegetable Crops Hotline: Copper products for bacterial spot of tomato
Plantwise factsheet: Protective sprays for bacterial spot on tomato

Tomato_Early_blight.name: Early blight
Tomato_Early_blight.summary: A fungal disease (Alternaria) that starts on the lowest leaves and moves up, favoured by warm, wet weather and overhead watering.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings (target-like) surrounded by yellowing
Lower leaves die and drop; stem and fruit lesions can also occur
Tomato_Early_blight.cure_note: Existing spots do not heal, but spread can be slowed and many plants tolerate a lot of early blight without losing much yield.
treatment: Catch it early and prune off infected lower leaves, but never remove more than about one third of the foliage
Wash hands and sanitize pruning tools after touching infected plants, and dispose of removed leaves away from the garden
Where disease pressure is high, extension services suggest a protectant fungicide program starting at fruit set on a 7-14 day schedule. Home gardeners often do not need fungicide
Keep leaves dry: water at the base, mulch and avoid wetting foliage
prevention: Choose resistant or tolerant varieties (often marked EB), though resistance is not immunity
Stake or trellis, space plants about two feet apart and remove the lowest leaves
Rotate out of tomatoes and related crops for at least two years and control nightshade weeds
Keep plants fed and watered; stressed plants are more susceptible

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension: Early blight of tomato and potato
Colorado State Extension: Tomato early blight
Oklahoma State Extension: Early blight of tomato

Tomato_Late_blight.name: Late blight
Tomato_Late_blight.summary: A very aggressive disease (Phytophthora infestans) of tomato and potato. It thrives in cool, wet weather and can destroy a planting in a few days.
symptoms: Large, irregular brown or burnt-looking patches on leaves, often starting at the outer canopy
Dark lesions on stems and large, firm brown blotches on fruit; white mold in humid conditions
Tomato_Late_blight.cure_note: There is no cure, and no tomato variety is fully resistant. Prevention and quick removal of infected plants are what work.
treatment: Remove infected plants promptly and bag or destroy them so spores do not spread (do not compost). Warn nearby growers, because spores travel on wind

Protectant fungicides only work if applied before infection; extension services advise a weekly program when weather favours the disease. Home gardeners can use fixed copper products (permitted in organic production)
Do not keep infected fruit for storage
prevention: Buy healthy transplants and destroy volunteer tomato and potato plants and nightshade weeds
Use drip irrigation, space plants and keep foliage dry
Some varieties are more tolerant, though none is immune

sources.title: WVU Extension: Late blight of tomatoes
UConn Extension: Late blight of tomato
UW-Madison Extension: Tomato late blight identification and management

Tomato_Leaf_Mold.name: Leaf mold
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.summary: A fungal disease (Passalora fulva) that is driven by high humidity, mainly in greenhouses and high tunnels, but also outdoors in long damp spells.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Olive-grey to purplish mold on the underside; leaves curl, wither and drop
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.cure_note: Infected leaves do not recover, but the disease can usually be stopped by lowering humidity and removing affected leaves.
treatment: Keep relative humidity below about 85%: open vents or tunnel sides, use fans and avoid wetting leaves
Prune and destroy early-affected leaves if practical, and thin the canopy for airflow
Foliar fungicides help when combined with the steps above; spray the leaf undersides and follow the label
prevention: Use resistant varieties (resistance can vary with local strains)
Space plants, avoid overhead watering and handling plants in humid conditions
Remove and destroy plant debris after harvest and rotate the growing location

sources.title: University of Kentucky PPFS-VG-52: Leaf mold of tomato
Ohio State: High tunnel disease facts, leaf mold
Cornell Plant Pathology: Leaf mold on tomatoes

Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.name: Septoria leaf spot
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.summary: A common fungal disease (Septoria lycopersici) that starts on the lowest leaves and climbs the plant in humid, rainy weather.
symptoms: Many small round spots with grey or tan centers and dark brown borders
Tiny black dots inside the spots; yellowing, leaf drop and sunscald on exposed fruit
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.cure_note: Spots do not reverse, but the spread can be slowed enough to protect most of the crop.
treatment: Remove infected lower leaves, avoid working plants while they are wet, and clear infected debris and nightshade weeds
Water at the base and prune the lowest leaf branches once plants are established
Fungicides used for early blight also work on Septoria; extension advice is a shorter 7-10 day interval, following the label
prevention: Rotate tomatoes away from the same spot for at least two years
Use disease-free seed; no variety is fully resistant, though some tolerate it
Shred and bury or hot-compost debris after harvest

sources.title: University of Maryland Extension: Septoria leaf spot of tomatoes
WVU Extension: Septoria leaf spot
Oklahoma State Extension: Septoria leaf spot

Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.name: Two-spotted spider mite (pest damage)
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.summary: Tiny sap-sucking mites (Tetranychus urticae) that multiply fast in hot, dry, dusty conditions and in drought-stressed or over-fertilized plants.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling on leaves, often starting on older leaves
Fine webbing, bronzing and leaf drop in heavy infestations; mites are visible on the undersides
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.cure_note: This is a pest, not an infection. It is controllable, and early detection matters most.
treatment: Check leaf undersides with a hand lens; act as soon as mites build up, before webbing appears
Spray leaves with a strong stream of water, and remove heavily infested leaves
Predatory mites (for example Phytoseiulus persimilis) are used successfully, especially in greenhouses and tunnels
If a miticide is needed, use one labelled for tomato, cover the leaf undersides well, and rotate products to slow resistance
prevention: Keep weeds down in and around the crop and avoid dust from mowing or traffic near plants
Water consistently and avoid over-fertilizing
Scout weekly in hot, dry weather

sources.title: University of Delaware Extension: Two-spotted spider mite
University of Maryland Extension: Two-spotted spider mites on vegetables
NC State Extension: Biological control of spider mites in tomatoes

Tomato__Target_Spot.name: Target spot
Tomato__Target_Spot.summary: A fungal disease (Corynespora cassiicola) common in warm, humid regions that is easy to confuse with early blight and bacterial spot.
symptoms: Small dark spots that grow into rings with a target-like pattern, starting on older leaves
Long thin lesions on stems; pitted spots on fruit
Tomato__Target_Spot.cure_note: Spots do not heal, but timely fungicide use and sanitation can limit spread.
treatment: Start protectant sprays when the first spots appear, using products containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb or copper where labelled for tomato, and continue until a few weeks before the last harvest
Remove lower leaves after fruit set and take out heavily infected leaves
Improve airflow with wider spacing and avoid excess nitrogen
prevention: Rotate for about three years before replanting tomatoes on the same land
Clear and burn or bury crop debris; do not plant new crops beside old infected ones
No commercial varieties are resistant, so rely on spacing, sanitation and dry foliage

sources.title: UF/IFAS EDIS PP351: Target spot of tomato in Florida
Pacific Pests, Pathogens and Weeds: Tomato target spot
World Vegetable Center: Target spot

Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV)
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.summary: A virus transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). Early infection causes the worst yield loss.
symptoms: Small, crumpled leaves that curl upward with yellow edges
Stunted, bushy plants with flower drop and little fruit
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.cure_note: There is no cure for an infected plant. Control means stopping whiteflies and limiting the virus source.
treatment: Remove and destroy infected plants early so whiteflies cannot pick up the virus from them
Control whiteflies with a labelled insecticide or biopesticide program, rotating modes of action. Treat adults before pruning or tying so they are not disturbed onto healthy plants
Reflective (metallic) mulch reduces whitefly numbers and virus spread
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant or tolerant varieties and use virus-free transplants; whitefly control is still needed with resistant types
Destroy crops promptly after harvest and control weeds that host whiteflies
Check the undersides of leaves for whiteflies regularly

sources.title: UF/IFAS EDIS IN1430: Managing Bemisia tabaci and TYLCV in Florida tomato
UF/IFAS: Management of whiteflies, TYLCV and insecticide resistance
Journal of Economic Entomology: Integrated management of TYLCV and its whitefly vector

Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.name: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV)
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.summary: A very stable virus spread mostly by hands, tools, seed and plant-to-plant contact. Mosaic symptoms can resemble other viruses, so lab testing confirms it.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green or yellow patterns on leaves, sometimes puckered or distorted
Stunted growth and uneven fruit ripening
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.cure_note: There is no cure and no chemical treatment for plant viruses. The only fix is removing infected plants and preventing spread.
treatment: Pull up infected plants including roots and bag or burn them; do not compost
Wash hands with soap and disinfect tools and stakes after handling plants, and work with healthy plants first
Avoid using tobacco products around plants and wash hands afterwards
Weed regularly, as weeds can hold the virus
prevention: Plant varieties labelled resistant to ToMV or TMV
Use certified virus-free seed or treated seed and buy transplants from reputable sources
Disinfect stakes, ties and equipment between seasons

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension: Tomato viruses

Tomato_healthy.name: Healthy leaf
Tomato_healthy.summary: No sign of the diseases this model knows about.
treatment: No treatment needed. Scout weekly, including the undersides of leaves
prevention: Water at the base in the morning and avoid wetting foliage
Stake or trellis, space plants and prune the lowest leaves
Rotate crops, clear debris at season end and choose resistant varieties
